headline: Isles of Shoals Cod on the Slack, Piscataqua Stripers Riding the Push
subhead: Thirteen miles of coastline is plenty when the ledges hold cod and the river's loading up with bass ahead of the Harvest Moon tides.
body_markdown:
People from away hear thirteen miles of coastline and figure there's not much to work with. That's fine by the guys who actually fish it. The Isles of Shoals alone have more structure per square mile than most 50-mile stretches of coast — Appledore, Star Island, White Island Ledge, Duck Island, the humps and hard bottom scattered between them — and if you know where the cod hold on the slack and where the stripers stage in the Piscataqua current, you don't need 130 miles to fill a box. This week proved it again.

Water's sitting in the low 60s along the coast and easing down a degree or two at a time, which is right on schedule for late September. That cooling trend is doing exactly what it's supposed to — pushing mackerel and peanut bunker south along the beaches and setting up the first real push of migratory stripers moving through behind them. We flagged this pattern two weeks back, said to expect gradual improvement in striper numbers as fall progressed, and that's exactly what the docks are reporting now. Numbers aren't blitz-level yet, but they're building day over day, and the Harvest Moon tides this week are going to accelerate that.

Out at the Shoals, the cod bite has been solid on the slack — not wide open, but dependable if you're on the right piece of bottom at the right minute. Boats working the ledges off Appledore and around Duck Island in 60 to 90 feet are doing best right at the tide change, when the current lays down enough to hold bottom without dragging a jig sideways. Diamond jigs tipped with a strip of clam, or a standard cod rig with fresh clam belly, have been the difference-makers. Fish to 8 and 9 pounds have come over the rail, mixed with a scattering of haddock on the same drifts. The window is short — twenty, thirty minutes either side of dead slack — so timing matters more than horsepower out there. Mackerel schools have been thick enough around the Shoals to jig bait right off the surface with a small tree rig, which is worth doing anyway since fresh mack strips are out-fishing store-bought clam on the bigger cod.

Back inshore, the Piscataqua is where the striper story is developing fastest. That river moves serious water, and the fish that are starting to filter south are using the current seams and back eddies around Henderson Point, Pierce Island, and the stretch below the Route 1 bridge to ambush bait getting swept through on the tide. Last two hours of the ebb into the first hour of the new flood has been the window — swimming plugs and soft-plastic paddletails worked slow along the seam, or live mackerel drifted on a fish-finder rig for the bigger fish holding deeper in the channel. Portsmouth Harbor itself has had scattered action on the same tide stages, mostly schoolies and a few keepers mixed in, nothing to write home about yet but trending the right direction as more bait funnels through.

Hampton Harbor is starting to show the pattern anglers wait all summer for. Incoming tide is pushing bait — sand eels and small pogies — right through the inlet, and stripers are stacking up on the edges of the channel and around the jetty rocks to intercept it. Bucktails in white or chartreuse, three-quarter to one ounce, bounced along the bottom on the last of the incoming has been the go-to, with topwater walk-the-dog plugs drawing some violent strikes right at first light before the sun gets up. Rye Harbor's seeing a similar setup at its jetty, with snapper blues thick enough now to be a nuisance for anyone targeting bass with anything smaller than a full-size plug — a good sign that bigger blues won't be far behind as more bait pushes down the coast.

Great Boars Head has been the better surf spot for stripers working the sand eel schools that show up on the outgoing tide, especially the last two hours before low. Metal — Deadly Dicks, Kastmasters, anything that mimics a sand eel profile — has outproduced bulkier plugs there all week. It's not a numbers game yet, more a game of being in the right stretch of beach when a school pushes through, but the fish that have come off that beach have been quality, mostly mid-20-inch schoolies with a few pushing into slot range.

Flounder have quietly been worth a mention too. The mud bottom stretches of Hampton Harbor and the slower sections of the Piscataqua are holding decent numbers on bloodworms and clam, fished on a simple two-hook flounder rig right on the bottom during the slower stages of the tide — an easy fallback if the bass and blues aren't cooperating on a given morning.

Looking at the next several days, the bigger Harvest Moon tides should keep doing what they're doing — moving more bait, sharpening the current at the river mouths, and concentrating fish more predictably around structure. If the pattern holds, expect the Piscataqua and Hampton Harbor bite to keep building through the week, with the better windows lining up around the tide changes rather than any particular time of day. Out at the Shoals, the cod bite should stay steady as long as the wind keeps the ledges fishable on the slack — worth checking the forecast before making the run, since that's an open-water crossing and not a day to force it in a chop. The next real acceleration in the striper run likely waits on the next cooling push, but the early signs are already there for anyone willing to read thirteen miles of coastline the right way.
